doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Learning arranging by brute force and Hollywood composers
summary: He learned arranging by fixing things and listening; recalls Steiner, Newman and boss Herbert Stothart at MGM.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Did you start arranging out of a kind of an innate interest in it or because it looked like something that you needed to do?

No. We called it “brute force school.” I started fixing things, as a rehearsal pianist, and then I think as you hear sounds and if you have fat ears and listen I think that’s the best teacher, in my opinion.
I know Manny Albam said the same thing.
Yes. He absorbed everything around him from all the different kinds of music he listened to.

Well you know I lived in Hollywood, in fact I saw — I was conducting in the south last night and I saw a friend, a gentleman that I hadn’t seen for a long time who was kind of an assistant director for Warner Brothers in the golden days. And we started talking about Max Steiner and Ray Heindorf and all of these people that I lived with every day, and never really knew how important they were and what a stroke they put on not only my life but the life of America. You know, Alfred Newman at Fox. And I worked for — my first boss at MGM was a man by the name of Herbert Stothart who did all the Nelson Eddy musicals so I learned all of that repertoire. Nelson Eddy and Jeannette MacDonald. That was my first training, but I read everything, no improvisation.
